misconceptions.statement: Bars in a bar graph can have different widths because only the bar's area matters.
misconceptions.why: Students treat bars like drawings rather than measurement marks, and see width as decoration.
misconceptions.fix: In a bar graph the height (length) shows the value, and all bars should have equal width and equal gaps so they compare fairly.

probe.question: A bar for Mon is wide and the bar for Tue is narrow, both reach 40. Which shows more?
probe.wrong_answer: Mon, because its bar is bigger

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger looking means bigger value

misconceptions.statement: Each square on a graph paper axis must always stand for 1 unit.
misconceptions.why: Students are used to rulers and number lines where each division is one.
misconceptions.fix: We choose a scale to suit the data, such as 1 square = 10 units, and keep it the same along the whole axis.

probe.question: Data values are 200, 400, 800. How many squares tall is the bar for 800 if 1 square = 1 unit?
probe.wrong_answer: It must be drawn 800 squares tall, so the graph cannot be drawn

misconceptions.root_belief: a scale always counts in ones
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' interpretation of scales and axes in graphs

misconceptions.statement: The numbers on an axis can be spaced unevenly if the data points are unevenly spread.
misconceptions.why: Students place labels only where data exists rather than at equal intervals.
misconceptions.fix: The scale on an axis must have equal gaps between equal steps, even where there is no data.

probe.question: Data are at 2, 3 and 10. An axis is labelled 2, 3, 10 at equal spacing. Is this correct?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, labels only need to be where there is data

misconceptions.root_belief: only what is present needs to be shown
misconceptions.source_hint: research on graph construction errors in school students

misconceptions.statement: A bigger sector in a pie chart always means a bigger number, regardless of the total of each pie chart.
misconceptions.why: Students compare sector sizes across two pies without noticing each pie stands for a different total.
misconceptions.fix: A sector shows a fraction of its own pie's total, so two equal sectors in pies with different totals stand for different amounts.

probe.question: Pie A (total 200 students) has a half sector for cricket; pie B (total 1000) has a quarter sector for cricket. Which has more cricket fans?
probe.wrong_answer: Pie A, since its sector is bigger

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger share always means bigger amount
misconceptions.source_hint: research on proportional reasoning and part-whole misreading of pie charts

misconceptions.statement: The angles of the sectors in a pie chart add up to 100.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up percentages, which total 100, with degrees.
misconceptions.fix: The sectors of a full circle have angles adding up to 360 degrees; their percentages add up to 100.

probe.question: Sectors are 30%, 20% and 50%. What do the central angles add up to?
probe.wrong_answer: 100 degrees

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-looking totals mean the same quantity

misconceptions.statement: To read a value on a line graph you read the number on the axis closest to the line, whatever the point is.
misconceptions.why: Students read off the nearest labelled gridline instead of following the point across to the axis.
misconceptions.fix: Follow a straight line from the point to the axis; if it falls between two labels, estimate using the scale of the small divisions.

probe.question: A point lies midway between the labels 20 and 30 on the y-axis. What is its value?

misconceptions.root_belief: nearest label gives the exact value
misconceptions.source_hint: research on graph-reading errors (interpolation) among students

misconceptions.statement: If the line on a graph goes up and then down, the thing shown is actually going up and down in height or distance like a hill.
misconceptions.why: Students read the graph as a picture of the journey instead of as a relationship between two variables.
misconceptions.fix: A graph shows how one quantity changes with another; a falling line in a distance-time graph means getting back toward the start, not going downhill.

probe.question: On a distance-time graph the line rises, then is flat, then falls. What does the flat part mean?
probe.wrong_answer: The person is walking on level ground

misconceptions.root_belief: a graph is a picture of the real thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on graph-as-picture misconception in kinematics graphs

misconceptions.statement: A steeper line on a graph always means a higher value, not a faster change.
misconceptions.why: Students attend to height of the line rather than how quickly it climbs.
misconceptions.fix: The steepness (slope) shows how fast the quantity changes; a line can be high but flat, meaning no change.

probe.question: Line A is high but flat; line B starts low but climbs quickly. Which one changes faster?
probe.wrong_answer: Line A, because it is higher

misconceptions.root_belief: larger value means faster change
misconceptions.source_hint: research on slope–height confusion in graph interpretation

misconceptions.statement: A line graph can be used to show any data, such as marks of different students in one test.
misconceptions.why: Students think joining points always makes a graph look better.
misconceptions.fix: A line graph is for data that changes continuously with time or another ordered variable; separate categories like students need a bar graph.

probe.question: Which graph suits the marks of five students, bar or line?
probe.wrong_answer: Line graph, join the marks of each student

misconceptions.root_belief: one method works for every case
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' choice of graph type for categorical data

misconceptions.statement: A pie chart can show how a quantity changes over many days.
misconceptions.why: Students think a pie chart is a general-purpose picture for any data.
misconceptions.fix: A pie chart shows parts of one total at a single time; change over time is shown with a line graph.

probe.question: Which graph best shows daily temperature for a week?
probe.wrong_answer: A pie chart with one sector for each day

misconceptions.root_belief: one method works for every case

misconceptions.statement: The origin is the point where the x-axis and y-axis end, at the bottom left corner of the page.
misconceptions.why: Students see only first-quadrant graphs in earlier work, so the origin is always at the corner.
misconceptions.fix: The origin is where the axes cross, with coordinates (0,0); the axes extend into negative values too.

probe.question: Where is the origin on a graph with both axes extending to negative numbers?
probe.wrong_answer: At the bottom left corner of the grid

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only picture
misconceptions.source_hint: research on coordinate-system understanding in school students

misconceptions.statement: All points with a negative coordinate lie in the same quadrant.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the idea of negative with 'left or below' and do not track both signs together.
misconceptions.fix: The quadrant depends on both signs: (-,+) is the second, (-,-) the third, and (+,-) the fourth quadrant.

probe.question: In which quadrant is (-3, -2)?
probe.wrong_answer: The second quadrant, since a negative number puts it to the left

misconceptions.root_belief: one feature decides a thing completely

misconceptions.statement: Quadrants are numbered clockwise starting from the top right.
misconceptions.why: Students associate clockwise with the clock and ignore the anticlockwise convention.
misconceptions.fix: Quadrants are numbered anticlockwise, starting with the top right as quadrant I, then top left, bottom left, bottom right.

probe.question: Which quadrant is the point (-4, 5) in?
probe.wrong_answer: Fourth quadrant

misconceptions.root_belief: turning direction is always clockwise

misconceptions.statement: The point (3, 5) and the point (5, 3) are the same point.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the pair like a set of numbers where order does not matter.
misconceptions.fix: Coordinates are an ordered pair; the x-value comes first and the y-value second, so (3,5) and (5,3) are different points.

probe.question: Are (2, 7) and (7, 2) the same point?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, both have the numbers 2 and 7

misconceptions.root_belief: order of items does not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on order and coordinate-reversal errors in plotting

misconceptions.statement: The first number in a coordinate pair tells how far up the point is.
misconceptions.why: Students link first with vertical because many measurement scenes begin with height.
misconceptions.fix: The first number (x) tells the distance along the horizontal axis; the second (y) tells how far up or down.

probe.question: Where is (4, 1) relative to the origin?
probe.wrong_answer: 4 units up and 1 unit across

misconceptions.root_belief: first means the vertical thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on coordinate-reversal errors in plotting

misconceptions.statement: A point on the y-axis has y-coordinate equal to 0.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up 'on the axis' with 'the value of that axis'.
misconceptions.fix: A point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0, like (0,4); a point on the x-axis has y-coordinate 0, like (4,0).

probe.question: What are the coordinates of a point 4 units up the y-axis?

misconceptions.root_belief: the name of a thing tells its value
misconceptions.source_hint: research on plotting points on axes in school coordinate geometry

misconceptions.statement: To plot (-2, 3) you count 2 units to the right because 2 is just a number and the minus sign can be ignored.
misconceptions.why: Students carry whole-number thinking and drop negative signs on the number line.
misconceptions.fix: A negative x-value means moving left of the origin and a negative y-value means moving down.

probe.question: Describe how to plot (-2, 3).
probe.wrong_answer: Go 2 to the right and 3 up

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: To plot a point, count the grid lines starting from where you put the pencil, not from the origin.
misconceptions.why: Students treat each point as a fresh start instead of a position from the origin.
misconceptions.fix: Each point is always located by starting at the origin and moving x units horizontally, then y units vertically.

probe.question: After plotting (2,3), how do you plot (4,1)?
probe.wrong_answer: From (2,3) move 4 right and 1 up

misconceptions.root_belief: each step starts from the last position

misconceptions.statement: In a table of values, the x variable and y variable can be swapped without changing the graph.
misconceptions.why: Students see the table as a pair of columns of numbers and not as input-output.
misconceptions.fix: Swapping x and y reflects the points and changes the graph; the independent variable goes on the horizontal axis.

probe.question: For distance = 2 × time, which variable is plotted on the horizontal axis?
probe.wrong_answer: Distance, either one is fine

misconceptions.root_belief: order of items does not matter
misconceptions.source_hint: research on variable placement on axes in graphing tasks

misconceptions.statement: A line graph of a linear relation should stop at the first and last plotted points.
misconceptions.why: Students think a graph only exists where they have computed points.
misconceptions.fix: The straight line can be extended on both sides because the relation holds for other values too (within the context).

probe.question: You plotted y = 2x for x = 1, 2, 3. Does the line pass through (5, 10)?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the graph only goes up to x = 3

misconceptions.root_belief: only what is shown exists

misconceptions.statement: Points on a straight-line graph can be joined freehand and any wavy curve through the points is fine.
misconceptions.why: Students see joining as connecting dots, not as drawing a straight line through them.
misconceptions.fix: For a linear relation the points lie on one straight line, which is drawn with a ruler; if they do not line up, one point is probably wrong.

probe.question: Three points of y = x + 1 don't look aligned. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Join them with a curve through all three

misconceptions.root_belief: connect the dots however they fall

misconceptions.statement: Only the points you plotted lie on the graph of the relation; other points of the line do not satisfy the equation.
misconceptions.why: Students see the line as drawn dots, not as every solution.
misconceptions.fix: Every point on the line satisfies the relation, and every solution gives a point on the line.

probe.question: The line y = x + 2 is plotted from points (1,3), (2,4). Does (10,12) satisfy it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it was not plotted

misconceptions.root_belief: only what is shown exists
misconceptions.source_hint: research on understanding graphs as sets of solutions

misconceptions.statement: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the object is moving at constant speed.
misconceptions.why: Students link a level line with steady or constant motion.
misconceptions.fix: A horizontal line means distance does not change with time, so the object is at rest; constant speed is a slanted straight line.

probe.question: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
probe.wrong_answer: The object moves at constant speed

misconceptions.root_belief: a graph is a picture of the real thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on misinterpretation of kinematics graphs

misconceptions.statement: A steeper straight line on a distance-time graph means a slower object.
misconceptions.why: Students think that rising more means more time taken.
misconceptions.fix: The steeper the line, the more distance covered in the same time, so the faster the object.

probe.question: Two lines on one distance-time graph; line A is steeper. Which object is faster?
probe.wrong_answer: The one with the less steep line

misconceptions.root_belief: more change in the picture means more time
